Beyond the final rank, the real trophy from BAJA SAEINDIA is the deep engineering experience. For my network of developers and roboticists, I wanted to share the core technical architecture that our team, Team Equinox, built to bring our autonomous vehicle to life.

My role was leading the Autonomous Systems Integration, the incredible challenge of bridging the high-level world of ROS 2 with the low-level reality of our vehicle's hardware. This was a journey in making two different worlds speak the same language.

Our entire system was architected around a central NVIDIA Jetson by Tanna TechBiz LLP running ROS 2 and connected to a Kvaser AB dual channel CAN adapter to interface it directly to the CAN network communicating with five distributed Arduino UNO R4 Minima microcontrollers over a robust CAN bus network. Each Arduino served as a dedicated, real-time "muscle controller" for a specific task (Startup, Dashboard, Throttle, Brakes, Steering).

This was a true team effort, and I was the fortunate integrator connecting the brilliant work of two major sub-teams:

First, the low-level Electrical Team, led by Naveen Shaji George and Muhammed Ajmal K with their incredible crew. They were the masters of the physical layer, designing the PCBs, building the complex wiring harness, and patiently debugging every circuit with me. Their work was the foundation everything was built on. When a relay fired unexpectedly or a sensor gave a noisy reading, they were the ones who found the solution in the hardware.

Second, the high-level Autonomous Software Team, led by ASHISH SHAJAN and Tomin Michael. They were the masters of the "brain," developing the perception and control algorithms in ROS 2. They gave me the high-level commands?the "what to do."

My job was to build the "how." This involved architecting the CAN protocol, writing the firmware for the Arduino nodes, and developing the central C++ ROS 2 can_interface node that acted as the real-time translator between the two worlds. The challenge was immense, from solving CAN bus arbitration conflicts to tuning PD controllers for our actuators and designing safety-critical state machines to pass the rigorous Technical Inspections.

The interface node includes converting the Starkenn Technologies Radar encoded CAN data to ROS messages through the DBC file. 

This experience was a profound lesson in how crucial the role of a systems integrator is. It's about understanding both the hardware and software worlds deeply enough to make them work together seamlessly. A massive thank you to both teams and many others who worked behind the scenes, for their collaboration, patience, and expertise. We built this together.

Media Description:
For anyone working with low-cost Mecanum-wheeled robots, accurate odometry without wheel encoders is a significant challenge. Standard kinematic models often fail to account for the real-world dynamics of continuous rotation servos, leading to severe drift.

To address this, I'm open-sourcing the complete ROS 2 Humble software stack for "Project Orion," a UGV I developed. This repository provides a working solution for robust localization on this challenging hardware.

GitHub Repository: https://lnkd.in/gEzjGPmv

Key Technical Features:
? Encoder-less Odometry: A forward_kinematics node that generates a stable wheel odometry stream purely from calibrated servo commands.
? State-Based Kinematic Calibration (SBKC): Includes the scripts and methodology we developed to tune the kinematic model for asymmetric drive mechanics (forward vs. strafing vs. rotation), significantly reducing open-loop drift.
? High-Fidelity URDF: A detailed XACRO-based robot model, including a kinematically correct pan-tilt mechanism and properly defined sensor frames (REP-103 compliant) for the HP60C RGB-D camera and IMU.
? Full Hardware Pipeline: Includes a complete, multi-tiered architecture for interfacing ROS 2 on an Orin Nano with a Teensy/Arduino for real-time control and sensor processing.

This project is for robotics students, hobbyists, and researchers who are building similar encoder-less Mecanum platforms and need a solid foundation for control and SLAM.

This work was developed as part of my internship at CSIR - National Aerospace Laboratories (NAL). Huge thanks to my collaborator Adithya Satheesh, who was instrumental in developing the 3D models and providing invaluable support throughout the project.

Feedback and contributions are welcome.

The spec sheet for a device like the NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano only tells half the story. To see what it's really capable of, We ran a series of CPU benchmarks across its different power profiles. We wanted to see the real numbers behind the marketing, and the results are telling.

The method was straightforward: use nvpmodel to select a power profile, jetson_clocks to lock the frequencies for that mode, and sysbench to run a 6-thread prime number calculation. Live stats were monitored with jtop.

Here's a direct comparison of the three key modes:

25W Mode: This is the default high-performance profile. It locks the CPU at 1.34 GHz and gives the GPU maximum priority. This scored 3448 events per second.
(Which is really interesting cause its supposed to be at 1.7GHz as I tested and confirmed with another Orin nano before. 
Any clues on why, maybe some config file bug or something else entirely.)

15W Mode: Interestingly, this lower power mode produced a higher CPU score of 3843 events per second. The jetson_clocks output shows why: it allocates less power to the GPU, allowing the CPU to lock in at a faster 1.5 GHz.
(Which is expected ofc)

MAXN_SUPER Mode: This is the unconstrained, "max-effort" mode. It removes the official wattage limit entirely. The result was a big performance increase, scoring 4437 events per second.
The most important finding came from running jtop in MAXN mode. The Orin Nano CPU pushed past its official 1.5 GHz specification, holding a completely stable 1.7 GHz on all six cores under full load. Total system power draw was a modest 11.1W for this CPU-only test, and the CPU temperature stayed at a healthy 71C. Plus the GPU was 1.02Ghz which is the max we found out.

And the last power mode which is 7W. which shows a 960MHz clock speed for only 4 active cores.(Which is the lowest anyway).

Thank You to my friend Sidharth Sajith for helping me test this out and made me familiar with many of the keywords here. 

Conclusion: The Jetson Orin Nano is an impressive piece of hardware with smart power management. The "best" mode really depends on your work. For a GPU-heavy AI task, the 25W profile is the way to go. But for CPU-bound work like compiling code, the 15W mode actually provides a faster CPU clock. And for short bursts, the MAXN mode shows what the silicon is truly capable of.

Media Description:
Why Our VSLAM Failed, and Why It's Our Biggest Success Yet

Over the past few sessions, I?ve been deep-diving into Visual-Inertial SLAM for our autonomous UGV, Project Orion. The mission: use an RGB-D camera and IMU to map and navigate an unknown environment. Our tool of choice: RTAB-Map in ROS 2.

To truly understand the limitations, we decided to stress-test the system in pure simulation ? no wheel encoders, no GPS, no depth fallback ? just visual-inertial odometry (VIO). And that?s where things got interesting.


---

? The Experiment

We isolated RTAB-Map's internal VIO for motion tracking. After days of tuning parameters, QoS settings, and TF frames, we finally had it running in Gazebo.


---

? The Outcome ("Failure")

VIO turned out to be incredibly fragile in simulation.
Fast rotations, sudden moves, or low-texture areas? Boom ? "Registration Failed".

Sometimes it recovered. But with each failure, drift accumulated.
The real kicker: after exploring the whole map, the robot returned to its starting point ? the visual system recognized it, but the backend rejected every loop closure.

Why? Because the odometry error had grown over 150x beyond acceptable limits. Closing the loop would have resulted in a broken, physically impossible map.


---

? The Insight ("Success")

This was actually the perfect failure. It confirmed something critical:
No amount of SLAM tuning can compensate for poor odometry ? especially when your only input is simulated VIO in an artificial, low-feature world.


---

? Real World > Simulation?

We strongly believe this fragility is amplified by the limitations of simulation. Real-world data ? with actual sensor noise, better lighting variety, richer textures ? could yield much more stable VIO performance.

Still, the lesson is clear:
The path forward lies in sensor fusion.


---

?? Our Next Move

We're building a robust odometry pipeline using an EKF, fusing:

Fragile but accurate VIO

Stable but imprecise wheel odometry

Complementary IMU data


This will give us a resilient foundation to support higher-level SLAM and navigation tasks.


---

? Calling All Experts!

If you?ve tackled VSLAM in real-world robotics or fought through odometry drift, I?d love to hear:

How did you overcome loop closure issues?

Have you seen similar VIO fragility in simulation vs real-world?

Any tuning or sensor tricks you wish you knew earlier?

From Chaos to Clarity: Building a Python Toolkit for Robust Computer Vision Datasets

Every great machine learning model is built on a foundation of great data. But in the real world, data is rarely clean, consistent, or balanced. I'm excited to share a project I developed to tackle this challenge head-on: a YOLO Dataset Toolkit.

This toolkit is a set of Python scripts designed to take on the "janitorial" work of data preparation, turning multiple, messy sources into a high-quality, training-ready dataset.

The Journey from Raw Data to a Perfect Training Set:

    The Challenge: We started by sourcing data from multiple public projects. Each came with its own structure, class names (stop vs. Red Light), and quality.

    The Problem: Simply combining these sources resulted in a severely imbalanced dataset, with some classes having 10x more images than others?a recipe for a biased model.

    The Solution: I built a configurable Python script that unifies the datasets. It uses a mapping file to standardize all class names and consolidate the data into a single, clean format.

    The Result: A perfectly balanced dataset, created by automatically under-sampling the majority classes. We went from a chaotic mix to a perfectly structured set, ready for training.

    The Extra Mile: To ensure quality, I even added an interactive OpenCV-based tool to let a human reviewer quickly spot-check images and flag any mislabeled data.

This project was a deep dive into the practical side of MLOps and data engineering. Building a solid data pipeline is a critical first step before any model training can begin, and I'm proud of the robust and reusable toolkit that came out of it.

When beta testing a global robotics framework, every single issue counts. For the new ROS 2 Kilted Kaiju release, my contributions just landed me in the top 3 testers worldwide, with 51 closed issues to my name. What an incredible journey! ?

The official release of the new ROS 2 distribution, Kilted Kaiju, on 23rd may is fantastic news for the robotics community. ?

I'm immensely proud to have participated extensively in the pre-release "Tutorial Party" testing event over the past couple of weeks. It was an intense and rewarding experience diving deep into the ROS 2 ecosystem on Windows.

Through this community effort, I was able to test and help validate numerous functionalities ? from core CLI tools, Python and C++ examples, to complex features like Quality of Service, Lifecycle management, SROS2 security, Composition, and Service Introspection with various RMW implementations (Fast DDS & CycloneDDS). This work directly involved identifying and reporting several bugs and setup issues, contributing significantly to the overall stability of the Kilted release.

It's truly humbling to see these efforts recognized, placing me 3rd among all the amazing contributors to the Kilted Tutorial Party! You can see the list in the image!

This experience was my first significant dive into open-source contribution at this scale, and it has been invaluable. I've learned so much about the ROS 2 architecture, the testing process, debugging in different environments (especially Windows with Pixi), and the collaborative nature of the open-source community. A huge thank you to the ROS 2 maintainers like Alejandro Hern?ndez Cordero, Tully Foote, Yadunund Vijay, Michael Carroll, Katherine Scott  and all others involved in this and fellow testers like Jatin Vira and Marlvern Chimbwanda  for their guidance and feedback along the way!

Looking forward to leveraging these skills and continuing to contribute to the robotics community. Congratulations to the entire ROS 2 team and Open Robotics on the Kilted Kaiju release!

My MPU6050Aries Arduino Library is Now in the Official Library Manager

So excited to share that my open-source Arduino library, MPU6050Aries, is now officially available in the Arduino Library Manager! This makes it super easy for anyone to install and use directly from the Arduino IDE.

This library is designed specifically for Aries boards (Vega/RISC-V architecture) and provides stable roll and pitch estimations from the MPU6050 sensor using a Kalman filter, along with temperature readings ? perfect for projects like self-balancing robots.

A huge thank you to FabLab Baramati  for reaching out, sharing how they've been using the library, and suggesting I submit it to the registry for wider community access. It's incredibly motivating to see your work being used and to be able to give back!
The process involved preparing the library, creating a release on GitHub, and submitting it to the Arduino Library Registry. It's a fantastic feeling to see it live!

?? Find "MPU6050Aries" in your Arduino IDE Library Manager or check out the repo: GitHub: https://lnkd.in/gfmEtH2f
